ledger.hypothesis: A phase profile of the original showed the finalize (20000 addElement + set3Double + outArr.set) at 2.1-2.9 ms of a ~3 ms tick, the latency-bound spring chain at 0.2-0.5 ms and the vector copy at ~40 us. The node is ELEMENTWISE (serial recurrence, no query, nothing cacheable: every input it reads moves), so the lever is per-access overhead: writing the existing elements in place removes a 20000-element allocate/free per tick, and emitting each element right after its spring lets the out-of-order core overlap the Maya calls with the chain's divide/sqrt latency. Accepted follow-ups, each A/B'd 3/3 with byte-identical fingerprints: layout checked once up front instead of elementIndex() per element; the min/max clamp if/elif turned into a select (the bench drives minDistance == maxDistance, so inside-vs-outside flips link to link and mispredicts, flushing the overlapped API work); spring rewritten on named scalars and the chain state carried in plain doubles across the opaque API calls. Also lifted the static NodeState registry to a per-instance member. Rejected: writing through asDouble3() instead of set3Double (slower 3/3), a bit-mask select (mixed), and writing through the existing array's own builder (addElement + set3Double, 2 calls instead of 3) -- slower 3/3, because addElement's index lookup costs more than next().
ledger.note: confirmed twice (incumbent under the noise floor): 0.787 / 1.105 ms
ledger.risk: The in-place fast path relies on Maya keeping array elements sorted by logical index (then first == 0 and last == n-1 means exactly 0..n-1); any other layout skips it and the original builder rewrites the whole multi. The branchless clamp keeps every comparison's type, direction and strictness, keeps if/elif precedence (min wins when both hold), and divides by 1.0 when length == 0 (x / 1.0 == x exactly). Outputs are byte-identical to the original build: all 20000 doubles x3 after warm-up, at n=37 and with 1 warm-up tick. Measured on this Windows box with an MSVC build (/O2 /fp:precise, the generator's recipe) run through the same harness arguments, because build.sh is macOS-only and bench.sh prints BUILD FAILED here. Original 1.25-1.87 ms vs final 0.67-0.83 ms (41-sample medians, noisy machine), so roughly 2x; the M4/clang ratio is unmeasured.
ledger.theme: Write the 20000-element driven multi in place, fused into the serial spring loop, instead of building and swapping in a brand-new MArrayDataBuilder array every tick.

ledger.hypothesis: Instrumenting compute() at 20000 links showed three serial costs on one thread: the latency-bound chain (~400 us; div -> sqrt -> div per link, irreducible without changing roundings), data.setClean(aDriven) (~380-1800 us, Maya walking 20000 connected element plugs), and 20000 in-place element writes (~170 us). setClean and the writes must stay on the compute thread (Maya API), but the chain is pure C++, so it can run concurrently with setClean; the critical path drops from chain + writes + setClean to max(chain, setClean) + writes.
ledger.note: Accepted by the optimizer at 4.11x, withheld in review: it runs the serial chain on a persistent worker thread while the compute thread calls data.setClean and writes the chunks the worker publishes -- a producer/consumer pipeline, outside the one threading shape the optimizer rules permit (a parallel map), and its setClean-before-write ordering was only checked in DG.
ledger.risk: Running data.setClean(aDriven) before the element values are written is new ordering inside compute(). It was verified in DG evaluation, but not under a parallel Evaluation Manager. The EM contract here: both calls still happen inside compute(), before it returns. Speed depends on the OS scheduling the worker on a P-core; on an E-core the chain can outlast setClean, and the progress hand-off only partly hides that.
ledger.theme: Run the inherently serial spring chain on a persistent per-node worker thread while the calling thread performs Maya's expensive attribute-level data.setClean(aDriven), then write the outputs in place chunk by chunk as the worker publishes them.

ledger.hypothesis: Instrumented phase timing (per compute, 20000 links) showed the worker takes 90-150 us to wake before the serial chain (358 us) even starts, while the caller idles, and the in-place writer (3 Maya calls per element, ~20 ns) then trails the chain by 75-450 us. Filling the wake gap with caller-side fused integrate+write, then a mid-chain handoff at link h (q of link h-1 passed under the mutex, 256-link publish chunks, bounded atomic spin before condvar), should cut roughly the wake lag off every tick while keeping one writer per link and one fixed integration order.
